text: The moth taped into the Harvard Mark II logbook on 9 September 1947 is real, but it did not give us 'bug'. The note, 'First actual case of bug being found', joked about a word engineers had used since Edison's day.
There is no reliable source for Bill Gates saying '640K ought to be enough for anybody'. He denied it in 1996, and quotation researchers have never found it in any contemporary record.
"We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil." (Donald Knuth, Structured Programming with go to Statements, 1974)

Dijkstra's 1968 letter 'Go To Statement Considered Harmful' was not his title. He called it 'A Case against the GO TO Statement'; the editor, Niklaus Wirth, renamed it, launching a genre of 'considered harmful' essays.
Tony Hoare added the null reference to ALGOL W in 1965 because it was easy to implement. In 2009 he called it his 'billion-dollar mistake' for the crashes and security holes it has caused.
"I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu) for 386(486) AT clones." (Linus Torvalds, Usenet post announcing Linux, 1991)
"A distributed system is one in which the failure of a computer you didn't even know existed can render your own computer unusable." (Leslie Lamport, email to colleagues, 1987)

The first known 'hello, world' program appears in Brian Kernighan's 1972 Bell Labs tutorial for B, the predecessor of C. Because a B constant held only four characters, the greeting was stored in pieces.
Graydon Hoare, who began Rust as a personal project in 2006, named it after rust fungi, a group of hardy plant parasites that he has called 'over-engineered for survival'.
In JavaScript, typeof null returns 'object'. It is a bug from the first implementation, where null, an all-zero value, matched the type tag for objects; fixing it now would break existing websites.
In 1994 Erwin Unruh showed the C++ standards committee a program that deliberately failed to compile: its error messages listed prime numbers. It revealed that templates could compute.
Go formats dates by example, using one fixed moment as a template: Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006. Written as 01/02 03:04:05PM '06 -0700, it simply counts from 1 to 7.
In 2013 researchers recovered a full 4096-bit RSA key from a laptop by recording the faint high-pitched noise its electronics made while decrypting. A phone placed next to the machine was enough.

The Morris worm of 2 November 1988 reportedly hit about 6,000 machines, a figure that began as a guess. Its author, Robert Tappan Morris, received the first felony conviction under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.
Public-key cryptography was invented twice. Clifford Cocks at Britain's GCHQ devised an RSA-like scheme in 1973, four years before RSA was published, but his work stayed classified until 1997.

Edsger Dijkstra designed his shortest-path algorithm in about twenty minutes in 1956, sitting on a café terrace in Amsterdam without pencil or paper. He said the lack of paper forced him to keep it simple.
The first web servers were never kept in a 'room 404' at CERN. Web co-creator Robert Cailliau has called the story a myth; 404 simply follows HTTP's scheme, where 4xx codes mean client errors.
The first message on ARPANET, sent from UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute on 29 October 1969, was meant to be 'login'. The system crashed after two letters, so the first word was 'lo'.

Ariane 5's first flight, in June 1996, ended about 37 seconds after launch. Reused Ariane 4 software tried to fit a 64-bit floating-point number into a 16-bit integer, overflowed, and the rocket destroyed itself.

Joseph Weizenbaum's 1966 chatbot ELIZA mostly turned users' words back into questions. Even so, he wrote, his secretary, who had watched him build it, asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it in private.

In 1951 MIT student David Huffman chose a term paper over a final exam: find the most efficient binary code. He found the optimal method, beating one his professor, Robert Fano, had developed with Claude Shannon.

SQL was first called SEQUEL, for Structured English Query Language. IBM had to drop the name because a British aircraft firm, Hawker Siddeley, held the trademark, which is why many people still say 'sequel'.

Python is named after Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake. Guido van Rossum was reading the show's scripts when he started the language and wanted a name that was short, unique and slightly mysterious.
C# was originally codenamed COOL, for 'C-like Object Oriented Language'. Its lead designer, Anders Hejlsberg, had earlier created Turbo Pascal and Delphi, and later led the design of TypeScript.

Jon Bentley found that about 90% of professional programmers could not write a correct binary search in a few hours. Java's own library version carried an integer overflow bug for about nine years until 2006.

AlexNet, the network that set off the deep learning boom, won the 2012 ImageNet contest with a 15.3% top-5 error, about 11 points ahead of the runner-up. It was trained on two gaming GPUs in Alex Krizhevsky's bedroom.
Shor's algorithm (1994) could break RSA on a large quantum computer, but demonstrations so far have factored only tiny numbers such as 15 and 21, and none has been a full, unsimplified run.

Classical statistics says bigger models overfit. Yet modern networks often show 'double descent': test error falls, rises near the point where the model can just memorize its training data, then falls again as it grows.
A Bloom filter, invented in 1970, tests set membership using a few bits per item. It may say 'probably yes' to something absent, but it never says no to something that is there.

Convolutional networks work partly because convolution respects symmetry: shift an image and its feature maps shift the same way. Geometric deep learning builds the same idea in for rotations, graphs and spheres.
